stories.title: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners over industrial capacity
stories.summary: Washington announced prospective import duties targeting 14 economies, including China and the European Union, following an investigation into alleged industrial overcapacity. The proposal uses a different statutory basis from the broad emergency tariffs struck down earlier in 2026. China disputed the rationale and the EU rejected the allegation that Europe causes structural overcapacity.
stories.whyItMatters: The proposal affects major manufacturing and consumer markets across Asia, Europe and North America and could reshape supply chains and trade agreements.
stories.selectionRationale: Broad direct cross-border economic reach, substantial independent coverage and a potentially enduring change to trade enforcement.
stories.evidenceNote: Three separately originated reports. The Guardian page was modified after cutoff; only the proposal and US statements corroborated in contemporaneous reporting are used. Reuters has an undated update indicator. Proposed ceilings, existing duties and potential uncapped rates are not conflated.

commonFacts.text: The US announced a tariff proposal covering 14 trading partners, including China and the EU.

framingDifferences.text: Disputed question: do foreign industrial practices justify this round of US tariffs? Position A: Greer in tr25-a argues that subsidies and other policies disadvantage US producers and warrant corrective duties, drawing on the trade office investigation. Position B: Guo Jiakun in tr25-b rejects China's alleged overcapacity as a pretext; the EU Commission separately denies that Europe is a source and prefers joint action. tr25-r establishes the proposal and China's objection, not the validity of the economic diagnosis.

The articles converge on the policy announcement, not on its justification. The EU accepts that global overcapacity can be a real problem, unlike China's categorical rejection. None demonstrates that these particular tariffs would correct it.

uncertainties: Final rates and exemptions after consultation.

Effects on industrial output, prices and international trade.

stories.title: Australia and Solomon Islands sign security and development treaty
stories.summary: Australia and Solomon Islands signed a treaty reinforcing Canberra's role in Honiara's security and providing for development cooperation. The deal restricts foreign military bases and addresses consultation on important infrastructure. The Solomon Islands government welcomed the reset while its opposition warned against abandoning security cooperation with China.
stories.whyItMatters: The agreement may alter strategic relationships across the Pacific and affects the island country's development options, policing and foreign-policy autonomy.
stories.selectionRationale: An international agreement with durable security provisions and implications for Pacific competition among major powers.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters, Guardian and ABC have distinct named reporting. ABC carries the opposition's prior warning in its November 25 report. Reports differ in confidence about the future of the China pact; Wale declined to discuss its disposition publicly, so definitive termination is not established. Local Solomon Star candidate was inaccessible and replaced with ABC's readable original reporting.

commonFacts.text: Australia and Solomon Islands signed a security-related treaty in Canberra on November 25.
The agreement identifies Australia as the preferred security partner and includes restrictions on foreign military or security bases.
The treaty accompanies Australian assistance for development and security, including education and policing.

framingDifferences.text: Disputed question: should Honiara prioritize Australian security cooperation while moving away from the Chinese pact? Position A: Albanese and Wale, reported in si25-a, portray the treaty as a stable partnership that respects sovereignty and provides tangible benefits. Position B: Sogavare, quoted in si25-b, argues that giving up the Chinese policing agreement could jeopardize development ties and reflects Australian influence. si25-r establishes the signed agreement but not the future effects or definitive status of the China pact.

The news reports converge on the strategic shift. Their quoted political actors disagree about whether that shift serves Honiara's interests. The funding provisions are evidence of commitments, not proof of delivery or the opposition's predicted harm.

uncertainties: Whether and when the previous Chinese security arrangement would end.
Whether the development and security commitments would be delivered.
Domestic political consequences and future relations with Beijing.

stories.title: Libyan army threatens retaliation and Italy criticizes Ukraine's strikes in Libya
stories.summary: Eastern Libya's military authorities said two naval officers had died of injuries from the Ukrainian attack on a Russian warship and threatened retaliation. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani criticized the operation as a violation of Libyan sovereignty, while Kyiv had defended it under the UN Charter's self-defence provision.
stories.whyItMatters: The diplomatic and military fallout raises the risk that the Russia-Ukraine war draws in other states and undermines stability in the Mediterranean.
stories.selectionRationale: Fresh escalation and a third-country diplomatic response following a cross-border attack; consequential for international law and regional security.
stories.evidenceNote: Continues the existing Libya event ID. AP's originating report was readable and original date corroborated via same-byline syndication, which is not a separate selected source. The Libyan casualty announcement is attributed; other selected reports do not independently confirm it. Kyiv Independent is a November 24 antecedent within the 72-hour source window. No legal adjudication established.

framingDifferences.text: Disputed question: does Ukraine's right of self-defence justify its military action in Libyan waters?
